abstract: This paper analyzes AI's employment effects using ADP payroll data from 2020-2025, finding a 13% relative decline in employment for ages 22-25 in AI-exposed occupations. The effects are concentrated in automation-oriented roles rather than roles emphasizing human-AI collaboration or augmentation, suggesting that AI's labor market impact is selective and depends on job task composition.
keyFindings: ADP payroll data shows 13% relative employment decline for ages 22-25 in most AI-exposed occupations compared to non-AI-exposed occupations.
Employment effects are concentrated in automation roles (where AI replaces human labor) rather than augmentation roles (where AI enhances human productivity).
Younger workers (ages 22-25) experience disproportionate AI-related employment effects relative to other age groups.
The study identifies variation in AI exposure across occupations based on task composition, with some occupations more vulnerable to automation than others.
Employment declines in AI-exposed occupations represent measurable early indicators ('canaries in the coal mine') of broader AI labor market displacement.
methodology: Analysis of ADP payroll data from 2020-2025, covering employment trends across occupations classified by AI exposure level. The authors classify occupations into automation roles (AI-replacing) versus augmentation roles (AI-enhancing) and measure relative employment changes by age group and occupational category. Sample includes millions of workers tracked through ADP's payroll processing database.
qualifiers: The study focuses on US payroll data only and measures correlation rather than causal effects. Results are specific to the 2020-2025 period and the ADP dataset, which may not capture all employment sectors equally. The paper notes that observed employment declines for young workers in AI-exposed occupations may reflect initial labor market adjustment patterns rather than long-term equilibrium effects. Limited sample for some occupational subcategories. The distinction between automation and augmentation roles, while analytically useful, depends on occupational classification which has inherent measurement limitations.
